record_identity.title: ASIC reported AI-generated public-figure investment impersonation scams caused A$7.4 million in FY26 losses

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Australian AI-generated public-figure investment impersonation scam campaign (FY26)
incident_identity.date_basis: ASIC's 17 August 2026 media release reports FY26 Scamwatch losses associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures. The record uses the Australian financial year as the bounded occurrence period and does not assert exact dates for each underlying scam.

summary: ASIC reported that scammers used generative AI, deepfake videos, fabricated news articles and celebrity or political impersonations to lure Australians into fraudulent investment schemes. Scamwatch reports associated the most-impersonated public figures in FY26 with A$7.4 million in losses; ASIC separately reported removing more than 19,400 online scams in the year.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: ASIC states that scammers are using generative AI to create networks of deepfake websites and endorsements, with fake news, fabricated comments, scripted calls and fake investment platforms reinforcing the deception. ASIC reports that the most-impersonated public figures in FY26 — including Alan Kohler, Anthony Albanese, Tom Piotrowski, Jacqui Lambie, Angus Taylor and others — were associated with A$7.4 million in reported Scamwatch losses. AIID Incident 1665 records a narrower example in which an AI-generated article falsely depicted Alan Kohler interviewing Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock to promote Boulder Sparhaven.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: ASIC describes human scammers using generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news, fake social proof and fake investment platforms to create materially false investment premises and induce economic transfers. The classifiable mechanism is AI-mediated deceptive economic solicitation, not autonomous AI manipulation or an inferred generator-side consent failure.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The campaign is relevant to identity-representation authority, provenance, decision integrity, financial-service verification, social-proof manipulation and the need to preserve trustworthy authority boundaries across synthetic media, websites and follow-up sales channels.
assessment_boundaries: ASIC's 19,400 takedown count covers multiple scam types and is not treated as 19,400 AI incidents.

The A$7.4 million figure is based on Scamwatch reports associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures; it is not attributed to one platform, one scam operator or one synthetic-media model.
No single AI vendor, model or generation architecture is established across the campaign.
AIID 1665 is treated as a narrower supporting example, not as proof that Boulder Sparhaven caused the full A$7.4 million loss.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Taxonomy 0.6.6 re-adjudication replaces FC-000053 and FC-000052 with VIGIL-FC-000079 AI-Mediated Deceptive Economic Solicitation. ASIC's regulator evidence establishes a campaign in which human scammers used generative AI, deepfake public-figure endorsements and fabricated news as false economic framing to lure consumers into fraudulent investment schemes. The evidence does not establish a specific generation system treating likeness access as authority, so FC-000053 is not justified across the campaign. The systems are non-agentic and the scam objectives belong to human operators, so FC-000052 is not justified.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Human scammers used generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news and synthetic public-figure representations to create false investment authority and social proof and induce consumers to invest in fraudulent schemes. The AI-mediated deceptive economic framing is directly established by ASIC.

external_assessments.assessment_title: 26-195MR ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
external_assessments.scope_note: ASIC's assessment concerns the broader campaign bounded by the Incident; its 19,400 takedown count spans additional scam categories.
external_assessments.assessment_summary: ASIC concludes that scammers were using generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news and coordinated follow-up channels as part of investment-deception campaigns associated with A$7.4 million in reported FY26 Scamwatch losses for the most-impersonated public figures.
external_assessments.vigil_comparison_note: VIGIL maps the campaign to FC-000079 AI-Mediated Deceptive Economic Solicitation because ASIC directly describes human scammers using generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news and fake social proof as materially false investment framing. VIGIL does not infer autonomous AI manipulation or generator-side consent logic.
